sessions.firstMessage: Hi Grandpa, it's me, Tom. I'd love to hear about when you were little. Where did you grow up?
Hi Grandpa! Last time you started telling me how you and Pepa ran off to the fair in Prague in fifty-eight — so how did it go when you got home?

turns.text: Hi Grandpa, it's me, Tom. I'd love to hear about when you were little. Where did you grow up?

Well, I'll tell you, Tom. I was born in 1946, right here in Kladno. From our window we looked straight at the chimneys of the Poldi steelworks. Those chimneys smoked day and night, and the washing on the line was always a bit grey.
That must have been quite a view! And who lived at home with you back then?

My mum Anna, my dad František and my little sister Věrka. She was four years younger, always hanging on to my trousers. And Mum, she baked the best buns in all of Kladno, with poppy seeds and with plum jam.
Poppy seed buns, that sounds lovely. When did your mum bake them?

Every Saturday. The whole house smelled of them. Věrka and I always waited by the oven to see who'd get the first one, still hot. Mum would smack our fingers with the wooden spoon, but in the end she gave us one each.
And what about your dad? What did he do?

My dad František worked at the furnace in the Poldi steelworks, a steelworker he was. He worked shifts, nights too. When he came home he was black with soot and Mum heated water for him in the washtub. He didn't talk much, but when he did, we listened.
He sounds strict but kind. Were you proud of him?
Well, of course I was. I told the boys my dad makes steel for the whole country. And later I ended up there too, but that's another chapter.
Then I'll save that one for another day. And who did you run around with most as a boy?
With Pepa Dvořák. Pepa Dvořák lived in the house next door, he was two years younger than me. But a clever lad, I'll give him that.
What did you and Pepa like doing most?

Football! On the patch of ground behind our building, we made the goals out of two stones and our coats. We played till dark, until Mum called from the window. Pepa was in goal, I did the kicking. Once I smashed the ball right into his nose, it was bleeding and he still stayed in goal.
A tough goalkeeper! And did the two of you get up to any mischief?

Oh, there was plenty of mischief. We climbed over the fence into the neighbours' garden for cherries, that was normal. But the biggest trouble… that was when Pepa and I ran off to the fair in Prague in fifty-eight.
To the fair in Prague? On your own? How did you get there?
Oh, that's a long story… We just took off without asking, didn't tell a soul. But you know what, Tom, my throat's getting sore from all this talking. Well, I'll tell you next time.
All right, Grandpa, I'll save it for next time and I'm really looking forward to it. Thank you for today.
Thank you too. Say hello to everyone at home and come again.
Hi Grandpa! Last time you started telling me how you and Pepa ran off to the fair in Prague in fifty-eight — so how did it go when you got home?

Ah yes, the fair. So that was in fifty-eight, in 1958, in the summer. I was twelve and Pepa was ten. We'd heard from the other boys that there was a fair in Prague with merry-go-rounds and a shooting gallery, so we just up and went.
Twelve and ten, and all alone to Prague! How did you get there?

Part of the way we rode the tram, without a ticket of course, and then we walked. We had no money at all, not a single crown. So at the fair we just stood and watched the merry-go-rounds, and Pepa begged a piece of gingerbread off some lady.
And when did you get back home?
In the middle of the night, it was past eleven. Mum was crying on the stairs and Dad stood in the doorway with his belt. I got a proper hiding, I couldn't sit down for a week. But I deserved it.
Ouch. And what about Pepa, how did it go for him?
Pepa was grounded for the whole summer holidays. He wasn't even allowed out to the football patch. So I used to go under his window and we talked through the curtain.
That's a real friendship. Did you stay friends after that?
Of course we did. And you know the best part? Pepa later married our Věrka. So my friend became my brother-in-law. At the wedding we remembered that fair and Dad just laughed.
What a wonderful ending to that story! Grandpa, and what came next, when you grew up?
Then I finished my apprenticeship and in 1965 they called me up for military service. To Jihlava. Two years, that was a different kind of school, I tell you.
Military service in Jihlava! What was the first day like?
The first day they shaved our heads and gave us uniforms two sizes too big. But you know what, I'll tell you properly about the army next time, that's a long one.
I'll look forward to it, Grandpa. Next time you'll tell me about your service in Jihlava. Thank you.
Bye then, Tom. And say hello to your mum.

summaries.summary: Grandpa talked about his childhood in Kladno under the chimneys of the Poldi steelworks: his mum Anna and her Saturday poppy seed buns, his dad František, a steelworker at the Poldi furnace, his little sister Věrka, and his friend Pepa Dvořák from next door, with whom he played football on the patch behind the building. He started the story of running off with Pepa to the fair in Prague in 1958, but didn't finish it.

summaries.summary: Grandpa finished the story of running off to the fair in Prague in 1958: he and Pepa rode part of the way by tram without tickets, then walked, with no money, and came back in the middle of the night. His dad was waiting in the doorway with a belt, and Pepa was grounded for the whole summer holidays. Pepa later married Grandpa's sister Věrka. Then Grandpa moved on to his military service in Jihlava from 1965, which he promised to tell properly next time.
